sourceBlocks.heading: Why sleep matters for learning
sourceBlocks.text: Learning does not end when a lesson ends. During the night the brain replays what happened during the day, and this replay decides how much of it is still there the next morning. This guide summarises a fictional classroom study that was written as practice material; its numbers are examples, not research results.

sourceBlocks.heading: What the study did
sourceBlocks.text: The study followed 120 students for four weeks. Each student learned 40 new vocabulary pairs on Monday evening and was tested on Tuesday morning. Half of the group was asked to sleep at least 8 hours, the other half was limited to 5 hours.
Every student wore a simple wrist tracker, so the hours of sleep were measured and not only reported by the students themselves.

sourceBlocks.heading: What it found
sourceBlocks.text: Students who slept at least 8 hours remembered 31 of the 40 pairs on average. Students who slept 5 hours remembered 22 of the 40 pairs. The difference of 9 pairs appeared in every one of the four weeks.
A short nap helped as well, but less. Students in the short-sleep group who took a 20 minute nap after school remembered 25 pairs, which is 3 more than without the nap.

sourceBlocks.heading: Three habits the students named
sourceBlocks.text:
No screens in the last 30 minutes before bed
The same bedtime on school days & weekends
Repeating the vocabulary once, right before sleeping

sourceBlocks.heading: What the study cannot show
sourceBlocks.text: The study lasted only four weeks and looked at one kind of material, vocabulary pairs. It may not hold for skills such as mathematics or sport. The students also knew which group they were in, which can change how hard they try.

sourceBlocks.heading: Takeaway
sourceBlocks.text: If there is one thing to remember, it is this: the hours of sleep after learning are part of the learning. In this study, three more hours of sleep were worth 9 more remembered pairs out of 40.
